cases.rationale: ...Rg5 catches the queen on d5. Qxg5 or Qxc6 gives up the queen for a rook. Qd7 allows a forcing double-rook sequence.
...h5 forces Rg4 to exchange for the other rook. The loss comes from the resulting pawn ending; there is no immediate gain in material.
Rb6 attacks the queen on c6. ...Qd7 saves the queen but allows Qxf6 because the queen ceases to guard the rook. A trap and a defender-overload explanation overlap.
Rh3 catches the queen on h4. ...Qxh3 gxh3 and ...Qh6 Rxh6 gxh6 both exchange the queen for a rook.
Bb4 catches the queen on d6. ...Qc5 loses to Bxc5+, while ...Qxb4+ axb4 salvages a bishop and check before ...exd5.
...Rbf8 catches the queen on f4 in the game continuation. Qf2 Qe3 preserves the queen through the checked horizon, but the pressure on the pinned queen and king remains severe.
Qf4 attacks the bishop on d4 and threatens mate. Even ...Bxf2+ loses the bishop, while ...Bxe5 and ...Bxb2 allow the short mate.
...Ne4 forks the queen and rook. Re2 saves the rook but lets ...Nxg3 take the queen.
...Rf6 threatens mate and produces a forced rook exchange into a lost pawn ending after Rxf6+ gxf6. This is a tactical liquidation with equal material.
...Na5 attacks both the queen on b3 and bishop on c4. The queen safely retreats to c2 and ...Nxc4 takes the bishop.
...Bg4 catches the queen on f3. Qxg4 Nxg4 is better than Qe3 or Qxf4, where the pawn wins the queen.
Bc3 catches the queen on b2. Even ...Qxc3 Nxc3 and ...Qxa1 Qxa1 give up the queen for less material.
Na4 catches the queen on b2. ...Qxa1 Qxa1 gives up the queen for a rook and ...Qb6 or ...Qb5 for less.
...Bd7 catches the queen on c6. Qxc5 Bxc5 limits the loss by salvaging a knight; Qxd7 also gives up the queen.
...Ba6 catches the queen on c4. Qa4 lets ...Bxe2 start a sequence that costs the queen, and Qxa6 Rxa6 limits the loss.
Be2 attacks the queen on g4. ...Qh4 Nd3 Qe4 keeps the queen through its first two moves. The subsequent ...Qxh1+ sacrifice is good practical salvage, but immediate queen confinement is uncertain.
...Kg7 catches the rook on h6. Rxg6+ Kxg6 costs the exchange of a rook for a pawn; Rh7+ or Rh8 loses the full rook.
...c5 catches the bishop on d4. Bxg7 Kxg7 or Bxc5 Nxc5 gives up the bishop for a pawn, and Be5 or Bf6 loses at least as much.
Ke7 catches the bishop on e8. Its only legal exits Bf7 and Bd7 both allow the king to capture it.
Na4 catches the queen on b2. ...Qxa1 Qxa1 concedes the queen for a rook; ...Qb5 and ...Qxd4 lose more.

limitations: One engine-assisted review. Paired root lines, unrestricted replies, and searches forcing each legal retreat of the attacked piece were checked before examining any classifier outputs.

Equal-material forced liquidations are tactical but are not scored as material traps. Prepared alternatives including ordinary forks and uncertain overlap are reviewed independently of the source tags.
This diagnostic overrepresents tactical errors. It does not estimate broad tactical precision or positional or mixed recall.
